passage: Tarun's interview was at nine, and at seven-fifteen the iron in the hostel broke. The only shirt he had left was crumpled, and it was pouring. Anand, his roommate, pulled a pressed white shirt from his own cupboard. "Take it. Go." Tarun checked his reflection: plain trousers, clean shoes, a collar that finally lay flat. He felt like a slightly different person and hoped it would help him say what he knew. On the bus he thought about how his marks had nothing to do with the shirt. In the waiting room he saw another candidate in a kurta and jeans, who seemed relaxed. Tarun realised that clothes told the panel something, but not everything.

qa.q: What time was Tarun's interview?
qa.a: His interview was at nine.

qa.q: What did Tarun feel about the borrowed shirt, and what did he realise on the bus?
qa.a: He felt more like a serious candidate and hoped it would help him speak, but he realised his marks had nothing to do with the shirt.

qa.q: What could Tarun do to prepare so that clothing matters less?
qa.a: He could dress neatly for the setting and put his effort into practising his answers about his work.

qa.q: How might the panel see a candidate in a kurta and jeans?
qa.a: They may see them as relaxed or slightly casual, but a first impression from clothing can't reliably show their ability.

grounding: Tarun dresses formally for an interview and recognises clothes signal respect but not ability.

passage:
Zainab laid out her clothes for the campus placement drive the night before: a navy blazer over a plain shirt, dark trousers, closed shoes. Aditi watched from the bed. "You look like you're going to a bank."
"That's the idea. The company sent a note saying smart formal." Zainab pulled her hair back. "I feel weird in it, but it tells them I took it seriously."
"Even if you're the best coder in the batch?"
"The clothes won't code for me." She smiled. "But I've seen people judged by what they wore, and it's not fair. So I dress for the room and then show them my work."
Aditi nodded. "Good luck. Text me after."

qa.q: What colour was Zainab's blazer?
qa.a: Her blazer was navy.

qa.q: Why did Zainab choose formal clothes even though she felt weird in them?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable in the clothes but chose them anyway because she wanted to show she took the drive seriously, as the company's note asked.

qa.q: What is the wise balance Zainab shows?
qa.a: She dresses to fit the setting and then relies on her work to show her ability, since clothes are not a fair measure of skill.

qa.q: How might a recruiter see a candidate who ignores the dress note?
qa.a: They might see it as not reading instructions or not taking the event seriously, though it doesn't say anything certain about their ability.

grounding: Zainab chooses formal clothes to show respect at a placement drive, knowing clothes do not measure ability.

passage:
"Suit or kurta?" Saurabh held up both on hangers.
Parul looked up from her laptop. "For the NGO interview? What did they say?"
"'Smart casual.' Whatever that means."
"Not the suit. You'll look like you're applying to a bank."
"The kurta, then?"
"The kurta with proper trousers. And polish those shoes; they've seen a war."
Saurabh laughed. "Does it even matter? They should care what I say."
"They will. But the first thirty seconds, they're also seeing whether you took it seriously."
"That's unfair."
"A bit. My cousin wore jeans to her interview and got the job anyway, because she was brilliant. But she said she felt small walking in."
Saurabh looked at the kurta. "I don't want to feel small."
"Then wear what makes you feel ready. And talk like you."

qa.q: What dress code did the NGO give?
qa.a: "Smart casual."

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling about the interview outfit?
qa.a: He was unsure and a little frustrated, finding it unfair that clothing might count, and worried about feeling small.

qa.q: What advice did Parul give, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: Wear the kurta with proper trousers and polished shoes, since clothes signal seriousness in the first moments, but then talk like himself.

qa.q: What does Parul's cousin's story show?
qa.a: That clothing is an unreliable measure of ability, since she got the job in jeans, but the wrong outfit can make someone feel small.

grounding: Shows a young adult choosing interview clothing to signal respect, while recognising first impressions from dress don't measure ability.

passage: At my first campus placement interview, I wore my uncle's borrowed suit, a size too big, and a tie I'd learned to knot from a video that morning. I'm Nitin. I felt like an actor. In the waiting room, I looked around and judged everyone. The boy in the shiny shoes looked like a topper. Payal, in a simple cotton kurta and flat sandals, looked, I thought, unprepared. I even felt a bit sorry for her. Then, in the group discussion, Payal was the best person in the room. Calm, sharp, she summed up everyone's points and fixed an error the shiny-shoes boy made. She got the offer; I didn't. On the bus home, I kept thinking about how quickly I'd sorted people by their clothes. Dressing well helped me feel serious. But it told me nothing about who could actually do the job.

qa.q: What did Payal wear to the interview?
qa.a: A simple cotton kurta and flat sandals.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Nitin felt humbled and a bit ashamed of how quickly clothes had been used to judge people.

qa.q: What lesson did Nitin take from the day?
qa.a: That dressing well can help one feel serious, but clothing tells little about someone's ability.

qa.q: How might Payal have experienced others' first impressions of her?
qa.a: She may have been underestimated at first because of her simple clothes, until her performance in the discussion changed that.

grounding: Shows a young adult choosing formal clothing for an interview and learning that first impressions from dress are unreliable measures of ability.

passage:
Placement officer's note, campus recruitment day, Thursday.
Varun, a final-year mechanical student, arrived for the engineering firm's interview in a clean but faded shirt, old trousers and shoes with a worn sole. I noticed one panel member glance at his shoes and then at me. Varun noticed too; his shoulders dropped. Before he went in, I spoke to him quietly and said the panel would judge his answers, not his shoes, and to sit up and speak clearly. His interview went very well. He solved the design problem faster than any other candidate and explained his college project on low-cost water pumps with real confidence. The panel offered him the job the same afternoon. Afterwards Akash, a junior volunteer, said, "I thought he'd be rejected the moment he walked in." I've reminded our volunteers that clothes signal effort, but they are a poor measure of ability, and that we should quietly help students with dress for future drives.
— Mr Chandra

qa.q: What was Varun's college project on?
qa.a: Low-cost water pumps.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when the panel member glanced at his shoes?
qa.a: He seemed self-conscious and discouraged, his shoulders dropping as he noticed the look.

qa.q: What did Mr Chandra do that helped Varun?
qa.a: He quietly reassured Varun that the panel would judge his answers, encouraged him to sit up and speak clearly, and later planned support with dress.

qa.q: How did Akash first see Varun?
qa.a: Akash thought Varun would be rejected the moment he walked in, judging by his clothes.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose worn clothes created a poor first impression that proved unreliable as a measure of ability.

passage:
Wednesday
Placement interviews today. I borrowed Didi's black blazer and ironed my one white shirt twice, because everyone says the first thirty seconds decide everything. In the waiting room most of us looked like a bank advert. Then Jagdish walked in wearing a faded kurta and rubber chappals, a cloth bag on his shoulder. I'll be honest: I thought, he's not serious, he won't get past round one. We ended up in the same group discussion. He spoke the least, but every time he did, the room changed direction. His point about delivery routes in hill towns was the best thing anyone said. Afterwards I found out his hostel had flooded and his only formal shirt was drying on a chair. He got shortlisted. So did I, thankfully. I'm glad I dressed with care; it helped me feel ready. But I judged a whole person by his chappals, and I was completely wrong.
Ira

qa.q: Why was Jagdish's formal shirt unavailable?
qa.a: His hostel had flooded and the shirt was drying on a chair.

qa.q: How did Ira feel after learning about Jagdish?
qa.a: Ira felt embarrassed and humbled at having judged him by his chappals.

qa.q: What balanced lesson does Ira take from the day?
qa.a: Dressing with care helped Ira feel ready and shows respect, but clothing is an unreliable measure of someone's ability.

qa.q: What might the day have been like for Jagdish?
qa.a: Probably stressful, arriving in a faded kurta after the flood among candidates in blazers, yet still speaking well enough to be shortlisted.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult dressing formally for an interview while learning that first impressions from clothing are unreliable measures of ability.
